title: A simple and practical correction procedure for non-uniformity of quantitative X-ray images that can be generated with an energy resolving photon-counting detector
abstract: : This study proposes a simple procedure for correcting non-uniform image artifacts in quantitative X-ray imaging using energy-resolving photon-counting detectors (ERPCDs) during non-destructive testing. Attenuation values (μt) l and (μt) h from low and high energy bins were modified by using correction coefficients α & β. First, to determine these coefficients, five carbon–aluminum combination phantoms were imaged, and effective atomic number (Z eff ) and effective mass thickness (ρ eff t) images were calculated for all patterns in which α & β were varied within the range of 0.90–1.10. Next, permissible regions were defined in the α-β coordinate plane where deviations from theoretical values were ≤2% for Z eff and ≤5% for ρ eff t. Then, for the regions where the two permissible regions overlap, the pair {α*, β*} which is the closest to {1, 1} was derived. These suitable pairs were calculated for each Z eff sample, and the correction coefficient functions of α(Z eff ) & β(Z eff ) were calculated for each image column. These correction functions were incorporated into the quantitative image calculation algorithm. As a result, our procedure reduced root-mean-square error by 78%–88% for Z eff images and 18%–68% for ρ eff t images. Furthermore, we demonstrated the effectiveness and feasibility of the proposed procedure using actual food samples.

title: Development and Experimental Characterization of Ti-Zr-Hf-Gd–Based High-Entropy Alloys Reinforced with Rare Earth Element Oxides for Advanced Nuclear Applications Through Nuclear Radiation Transmission, Phase Stability, and Nanostructure Control
abstract: This study designs and evaluates Ti-Zr-Hf-Gd–based high-entropy alloy (HEA) matrix composites prepared with three different rare earth oxide additions, namely Sm2O3, Er2O3, and Eu2O3, as multifunctional candidate materials for nuclear- and radiation-related applications. The rare earth oxide additions were selected because of their potential contribution to photon attenuation and neutron interaction behavior.X-ray diffraction analysis revealed that the alloying strategy strongly influenced the resulting phase constitution. The Nb-containing TiZrHfGdNbEr2O3 composition promoted a highly crystalline body-centered-cubic–dominated structure, whereas the B-containing TiZrHfGdBSm2O3 and TiZrHfGdBEu2O3 alloys exhibited dominant hexagonal close packed (hcp)-type features with broadened diffraction peaks, indicating refined or nanocrystalline structures associated with boride-related phase formation.scanning electron microscopy/energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy analyses showed a relatively uniform elemental distribution in the Nb-Er2O3–containing alloy, while the B-containing alloys displayed localized Ti- and Zr-rich partitioning within the secondary phase regions, supporting the possible formation of hard (Ti,Zr,Hf)B2–type precipitates. Vickers microhardness measurements further confirmed a composition-dependent mechanical response, with the highest hardness observed for the Nb-containing alloy.Gamma-ray attenuation experiments using a 133Ba source confirmed that all the fabricated alloys exhibited effective shielding behavior within the measured photon energy range up to 383 keV, although the relative mass attenuation coefficient, linear attenuation coefficient, and half-value layer rankings varied with photon energy.In addition, theoretical EpiXS-based mean free path benchmarking suggested that the Eu2O3–containing alloy may provide favorable calculated attenuation behavior compared with AISI (American Iron and Steel Institute) 316 and Inconel 600/625 in the 0.5- to 2-MeV range; however, this comparison, which should be regarded as predictive screening, requires future experimental validation at higher gamma-ray energies.Fast neutron experiments under 241Am/Be exposure showed absorbed dose rate reductions of up to 56.7%, indicating the neutron attenuation capability of the developed compositions under the employed experimental conditions. Nevertheless, neutron activation of Hf-, Gd-, and Er-containing systems remains an important consideration for long-term nuclear service use and should be assessed through isotope-specific activation studies.Overall, the developed HEA composites demonstrated composition-dependent phase formation, microstructural features, microhardness behavior, and combined gamma/neutron attenuation potential, supporting their further investigation as advanced radiation shielding materials.

title: Overcoming the Limitations of the Conventional Point Model in Neutron Multiplicity Measurement Using a Deep Learning Framework
abstract: Reliable non-destructive assay of nuclear materials remains essential for nuclear safeguards, security, and criticality-safety applications as nuclear energy systems continue to diversify. Particularly for fissile material assay, conventional neutron multiplicity analysis has long relied on point model-based formulations, but its accuracy is limited by simplified assumptions, and sample geometry-dependent biases. This study presents an alternative methodology via deep learning to overcome such limitations and to improve the estimation of fission rate F , neutron multiplication factor M , and sample’s mass beyond point model analyses. The proposed C2C-GRU (Coordinate-to-Context Gated Recurrent Unit) framework directly utilizes sequential particle-tracking data generated through Monte Carlo N-Particle simulations to represent detector responses. By minimizing extensive post-processing, the framework reduces information loss that occurs when detector responses are compressed into consolidated multiplicity count rates. Under passive neutron conditions, the symmetric mean absolute percentage error for M is reduced from about 22% to the order of 1% and for F from about 22% to about 8%. We also found that the relative performance trends obtained with C2C-GRU across different assay modes were consistent with established physical understanding. These results demonstrate the feasibility of a deep learning-based multiplicity analysis methodology for improving fissile material characterization beyond conventional point-model analysis.

title: Integrated dose-rate mapping and hotspot localization with a UAV-mounted coded-aperture gamma camera
abstract: Rapid remote radiation monitoring is important for identifying contaminated regions while reducing personnel exposure. This study developed an unmanned aerial radiation monitoring system (UARMS) equipped with a coded-aperture gamma camera and evaluated a staged workflow integrating flight-based spatial screening with hovering-based gamma-ray imaging. A controlled outdoor experiment was conducted using 60 Co and 137 Cs point sources. The flight-based survey identified two candidate source-related regions, and the corresponding region-of-interest spectra showed photopeaks of the two sources. The UARMS and ground-based backpack surveys showed broadly corresponding spatial patterns, although their relative intensities and spatial extents differed. During hovering measurements, gamma-ray images corresponding to the two source directions were reconstructed, and ambient dose equivalent rates were estimated. A comparison of altitude-only, image-derived, and UAV-GNSS-referenced distance corrections showed that the horizontal source offset affected the estimates but did not consistently improve agreement with the theoretical source-only values for both sources. These results demonstrate the field feasibility of sequentially performing spatial screening, radionuclide identification, hotspot localization, and ambient dose equivalent rate estimation using a single coded-aperture gamma camera under controlled point-source conditions.

title: The impact of a hypothetical nuclear explosion’s source region electromagnetic pulses (SREMP) on urban communications infrastructure
abstract: This study aims to evaluate the effects of nuclear electromagnetic pulses, with a particular focus on source region electromagnetic pulses (SREMP), on essential urban infrastructure, notably telecommunications systems. Through systematic analysis, the investigation seeks to clarify the extent of disruption and the vulnerabilities SREMPs pose to urban communication networks, contributing to a deeper understanding of critical infrastructure resilience in the face of such electromagnetic threats. These pulses, generated by nuclear detonations, can severely disrupt urban environments. The research aims to determine the extent of areas affected by explosions of varying yields and how detonation locations influence the resilience of telecommunications infrastructure, particularly by comparing antenna density in impacted regions with the total number in the area. Adopting a conservative approach, the study assesses the vulnerability of this infrastructure while excluding it from the analysis. Using HotSpot Health Physics Codes for simulations, it examines relationships among explosion yields, the range of electromagnetic effects, and antenna density. Findings emphasize the importance of maintaining communication for survival after such events and highlight the need to develop protective strategies to enhance urban resilience against disruptions, intentionally excluding thermal effects, radiation emissions, mechanical impacts, and biological consequences.

title:
Improvements to In-Canal Assay of High Specific Activity
                    <sup>60</sup>
                    Co at the Advanced Test Reactor
abstract: Improvements to the quality of measurements in the assaying of high specific activity (HSA) 60Co produced at the Advanced Test Reactor (ATR) at the Idaho National Laboratory are reported. Such assays are conducted regularly between cycles at the ATR, and because of radiological safety concerns, they are performed within the ATR canal. A standard ion chamber detector is placed in a collimated assay tube within the canal. Another tube, parallel to the detector, is used to position various 60Co standards and targets. The collimated port between these tubes allows for the targets to be pulled across the collimator via a winch system. Previous measurements were performed at discrete 1.5-in. steps using a hand-cranked winch system. Charge was collected and integrated for 10 s at each discrete step during a scan. Two substantial improvements to the assay include an electronically controlled, motor-driven winch system and a software-controlled continuous charge collection. Combined, these changes improved the quality of measurements as well as streamlined the assay process.

title: Uncertainty and Sensitivity Analysis of the QUENCH-06 Experiment Using PISAA Code
abstract: A severe accident code, program integrated for severe accident analysis (PISAA), was developed for the safety assessment of domestic nuclear power plants. To evaluate its capability in simulating fuel bundle behavior during the core heat-up and reflood phases, a series of input decks for the QUENCH-06 facility were developed and simulated using the PISAA code. The objective was to investigate the influence of nodalization, oxidation models, and heat transfer on key outputs. The nodal sensitivity shows that core nodalization has a significant influence on hydrogen mass and temperature distribution. Comparative results indicate that the 4-ring, 64-level nodalization scheme can generally capture temperature trends at different axial locations, although temperatures in the lower and intermediate regions of the test section are clearly overestimated, leading to a corresponding overestimation of oxide thickness in these regions. Furthermore, uncertainty analysis indicates that both hydrogen mass and oxide thickness are affected by the oxidation models, and that inter-node radial heat transfer has the most significant influence among all uncertain inputs. Therefore, it is concluded that, with an appropriate nodalization input deck, the PISAA code is capable of capturing the temperature distribution and the amount of hydrogen in the QUENCH-06 experiment.

title: Progress in the development of the cooling plate fabrication process and welding technology for the HCCP TBM breeder unit
abstract: The Helium Cooled Ceramic Pebble (HCCP) Test Blanket Module (TBM) is being developed jointly by Europe and Korea, with ITER Korea in charge of the breeder unit (BU) including its cooling plates. As an alternative to the special electrical discharge machining process, a cooling plate fabrication process combining conventional machining and hot-press diffusion bonding was developed, in which EUROFER97 was bonded at 1150 °C and 12.5 MPa for 3 h. Diffusion-bonded joints were fabricated and evaluated with initial post-bonding heat treatments, and eight heat treatment conditions were then screened on base metal specimens subjected to the bonding and heat treatment histories; double normalizing followed by single tempering with air cooling satisfied the RCC-MRx tensile, impact, hardness and grain size requirements. For the U-bending process, die press bending was selected over 3-point bending, and a finite element analysis identified the gap remaining at the end of bending as the dominant parameter; the improved dies achieved a curvature tolerance below 2.5 mm and a springback below 1 mm with a single press. For the BU welding, eight welding groups were defined from the assembly sequence, bead-on-plate tests with three laser systems showed that the welding motion and the shielding method are critical factors, and the applicability of the wobble function to the RAFM steel was confirmed.

title: Experimental evaluation of Simplified Radionuclide Transport model predictions for pool scrubbing: Importance of inlet particle size distributions
abstract: This study demonstrates that incorporating detailed initial particle size distributions into pool scrubbing models is effective for improving the accuracy of decontamination factor (DF) predictions under severe accident conditions in nuclear reactors. To overcome the significant uncertainties of conventional single-representative-diameter models, we investigated the size-integrated DF approach incorporating the initial particle size distribution using the Simplified Radionuclide Transport (SRT) model, evaluated against pool scrubbing experiments conducted under low-velocity gas injection conditions using Cu and Al aerosols. The results showed that while DFs increased with pool depth for both aerosols, the conventional single-representative-diameter model severely overestimated DFs at deeper pool levels. In contrast, the size-integrated DF approach incorporating the initial particle size distribution successfully reproduced the experimental trends. This result is consistent with the physical behavior in which large particles with high removal efficiency are captured at an early stage, while submicron particles, which are difficult to remove at greater depths, are concentrated within the bubbles. At the maximum pool depth, the deviations between the size-integrated DF and the experimental DF were -55% for Cu and -11% for Al.

title: Combined aberration correction strategy with toroidal ESA and sextupole lenses for high-resolution double-focusing mass spectrometers
abstract: Achieving high resolution in double-focusing mass spectrometers requires effective suppression of second-order aberrations, yet the relationship between the electrostatic analyzer (ESA) field profile and second-order aberrations remains insufficiently quantified. This paper proposes a combined aberration correction strategy based on a toroidal ESA and sextupole lenses: an analytical multipole expansion model of the toroidal ESA is first introduced, giving a quantitative link between toroidal factor 𝑐 and the quadrupole 𝑛 1 , sextupole 𝑛 2 components. This model enables rapid parameter scanning for first-order ion-optics design without repeated finite element method (FEM). Afterwards, three candidate sextupole lens configurations are evaluated, and a differential evolution algorithm is used to optimize the lens arrangement for second-order aberration correction. The proposed strategy is validated on a reversed Nier–Johnson geometry design through ion-optics optimization, FEM field simulation, and multi-particle tracking. The design yields an RMS spot size of 2 . 0 8 μ ⁢ m and a mass resolving power of 17,300, which demonstrate that the proposed strategy provides a computationally efficient ion-optical design route for high-resolution double-focusing mass spectrometers.

title: A hybrid Monte Carlo–nodal–machine learning framework for fast intra-pin power prediction in the PRATIC benchmark
abstract: Accurate prediction of intra-pin power distributions can be challenging for state-of-art nodal diffusion solvers, particularly in cores exhibiting strong spatial heterogeneities such as boron-free small modular reactors. Under such conditions, pin power reconstruction methods may not fully capture the potential presence of highly localised flux gradients, leading to biased heat flux and neutron fluence estimates. While Monte Carlo methods can resolve these effects, their computational cost limits their applicability for routine core-follow analyses. This work investigates data-driven surrogate models as a computationally efficient alternative to MC simulations for intra-pin power estimation. The study is based on a depletion calculation of a two-dimensional version of the PRATIC boron-free PWR SMR benchmark, analysed within the Kraken multi-physics framework. For that purpose, the core was consistently modelled with the MC Serpent code and the ANTS diffusion solver to generate a detailed intra-pin power dataset used for surrogate model training under nominal operating conditions. Two modelling approaches were considered: a multivariate linear regression model and a feed-forward neural network (NN), both using rapidly available nodal outputs such as pin power or pin burnup as input. The linear model achieved a coefficient of determination of R 2 = 0.97030 on the test dataset, indicating reasonable predictive capability but limited ability to capture nonlinearity effects. In contrast, the NN significantly improved performance, achieving a R 2 = 0.99962 and reducing the root mean square error by nearly an order of magnitude. The NN predictions showed excellent agreement with MC reference data, with a mean relative deviation of ( 0.02 ± 0.85 ) % , while maintaining prediction times on the order of seconds compared to several days for MC simulations. This study demonstrates the potential of surrogate models to provide rapid intra-pin power estimates across burnup states for the investigated benchmark within the validity envelope of the operating conditions used to generate the training dataset (all rod out, equilibrium xenon, fixed thermal-hydraulic conditions, and burnup states up to 17.5 MWd/kgU). Future developments incorporating a wider range of operating conditions and core states into the training dataset could further extend this validity envelope and enhance the model’s applicability to online core monitoring, as well as to the design, monitoring, and evaluation of fuel material irradiation programmes.

title: Single-bubble rise in liquid metals: CFD modeling, validation, and correlation assessment
abstract: This work presents a detailed numerical analysis of the rising motion of single bubbles in stagnant liquid metals (LM) over bubble diameters [[EQUATION]]. Simulations were performed using the geometric Volume-of-Fluid (VOF) method implemented in the open-source computational fluid dynamics (CFD) code OpenFOAM. Four bubble–LM systems of nuclear relevance were considered: helium in lead–lithium eutectic (He/LLE), steam in lead–bismuth eutectic (Steam/LBE), nitrogen in LBE (N₂/LBE), and nitrogen in mercury (N₂/Hg). The CFD model was validated against benchmark experimental data for N₂/Hg, yielding a mean absolute relative deviation (MARD) of 4.0%.The simulations revealed distinct trajectory regimes: small bubbles followed oscillatory zigzag paths, whereas larger bubbles rose predominantly vertically. Terminal velocities followed the trend He/LLE (187–206 mm/s) > Steam/LBE (180–185 mm/s) > N₂/LBE (178 mm/s) > N₂/Hg (175–180 mm/s). Notably, velocities for steam bubbles in LBE were up to ~30% lower than reported values from similarity experiments in transparent liquids, suggesting more conservative design margins are required for lead-based reactors. Sixteen published correlations were assessed (terminal-velocity and drag-coefficient models). Most terminal-velocity correlations predicted within 10–20% deviation, with Maneri and Vassallo (2000) performing best (MARD = 8.9%). Drag-coefficient correlations were generally less accurate; Yan et al. (2018) provided the highest predictive capability (MARD = 2.9%). This study provides reference data and a tested methodology for single-bubble dynamics in liquid metals, informing correlation selection and safety analyses in advanced fission and fusion systems.

title: Criticality and sensitivity/uncertainty analysis of spent nuclear fuel dry casks
abstract: Dry storage systems are considered worldwide as the main solution to store spent nuclear fuel outside the spent fuel pools of nuclear power plants. In these storage systems, re-criticality conditions must be avoided during the storage and transport of spent nuclear fuel. In this work, it has been found out that only for PWR casks re-criticality conditions can happen, under realistic conditions in case of cask internal flooding with natural water, while for BWR casks it has not been found out, under realistic conditions. Therefore, this work reports the criticality and sensitivity/uncertainty analysis of these systems carried out within the EU EURAD project, proposing some solutions to improve the safety levels.

title: Numerical Investigation of Boiling and Two-Phase Natural Circulation in a Full-Scale Core Catcher Using OpenFOAM
abstract: The core catcher system is designed to cool molten corium relocated outside the reactor pressure vessel during a severe accident in a nuclear power plant. The relocated corium imposes a heat load on the core catcher, which induces boiling and two-phase flow within the cooling channels. This process drives a natural circulation flow that facilitates the overall cooling process. Understanding these complex thermal-hydraulic phenomena, particularly the two-phase flow characteristics within the channels, is essential for ensuring the long-term cooling efficacy and structural safety of the core catcher system. The primary goal of this study is to conduct an in-depth numerical analysis of the thermal-hydraulic phenomena within a full-scale core catcher design using the OpenFOAM CFD framework. To ensure the credibility of the simulation, the selected physical models were validated against experimental datasets obtained from the VPEX facility. Based on the validated computational platform, the investigation was scaled up to a three-dimensional domain representing the complete geometry of the core catcher.

title: Technical Note: Thermal Signatures for Safeguarding Dry Storage Casks
abstract: This technical note evaluates the feasibility of using canister-surface thermal signatures as an indirect safeguards indicator for spent nuclear fuel dry storage casks. A computational thermal model of a horizontal NUHOMS-type dry storage module was used to examine diversion-relevant scenarios in which selected fuel assemblies were either removed or replaced by lower-power dummy assemblies. Temperature distributions on the canister surface were compared against the normal loading condition using distributed line-probe data intended to represent fiber-optic temperature measurements. The results show that changes in assembly heat generation produce localized and spatially structured temperature deviations on the canister surface, with the magnitude and pattern depending on the assembly location and diversion scenario. These results suggest that distributed thermal monitoring could provide a complementary, non-intrusive signature for verifying dry cask contents and maintaining continuity of knowledge during extended storage. The method is not proposed as a standalone safeguards technology, but as a practical supplemental signature that may enhance existing radiation-based, visual, and containment/surveillance approaches.

title: Study on the material and optical properties of silica aerogel used as a Cherenkov radiator
abstract: The detection of gamma rays with different energies in inertial confinement fusion is important for resolving the evolution of the fusion process. This work addresses two primary objectives. First, irradiation stability is tested through the change in wavelength-dependent transmittance before and after irradiation. Quantitatively, two separately prepared 100 mg/cm 3 tiles were measured from 250 to 650 nm after cumulative 60 Co gamma-ray doses up to 1.402 kGy; the largest changes occurred below 350 nm, while the visible-range response remained close to the unirradiated level. Second, the temporal and spectral responses of the aerogel measurement system are evaluated. The PMT225-based system had measured rise times of 0.3981-0.4025 ns with a maximum uncertainty of 1.1%, and the corrected relative spectral-energy distribution followed a power law with an exponent of −3.001 ± 0.434. The refractive indices of 30 and 120 mg/cm 3 aerogels at 632.8 nm were 1.005 and 1.028, corresponding to electron threshold energies of 4.618 and 1.690 MeV, respectively. Geant4 calculations and measurements with 1-3 cm tiles under 9.6 MeV electron irradiation agreed within a maximum relative difference of 15.48%. These results provide a quantitative basis for using density-tunable silica aerogel as a Cherenkov radiator in high-energy gamma-ray diagnostic systems.
title_ko: 체렌코프 라디에이터로 사용되는 실리카 에어로겔의 재료 및 광학적 특성에 관한 연구

title: Ring Oscillator-Based FPGA Online Localized Temperature Monitoring for Nuclear Safety-Class DCSs in Nuclear Power Plants
abstract: Accurate thermal analysis of field programmable gate array (FPGA) chips is critical for ensuring the reliability of nuclear safety-class distributed control systems (DCSs), especially under high-load and complex operating conditions. In this work, an on-chip localized temperature monitoring method based on ring oscillator (RO) is proposed. An RO array is constructed using the internal carry-chain resources of the FPGA, exploiting the temperature sensitivity of logic gate propagation delay to enable quasi-real-time, on-chip monitoring of localized thermal variations. Experiments are conducted at ambient temperatures ranging from 20°C to 60°C to acquire and analyze the frequency response characteristics of the ROs under different operating conditions. A three-dimensional thermal model of the FPGA board is established using finite element analysis (FEA), with the XADC temperature measurement providing a constraint for estimating the relative spatial temperature distribution within the FPGA. The results demonstrate that the proposed empirical frequency–temperature response model can consistently characterize the measured RO frequency variations under the investigated thermal conditions. By exploiting the on-chip RO array, the proposed method supports quasi-real-time monitoring of localized thermal variations without requiring external temperature sensors or dedicated acquisition hardware during operation. For hotspot regions exhibiting non-monotonic frequency responses, the RO outputs are used as relative indicators of localized thermal variation rather than being converted into unique absolute-temperature estimates. The implementation introduces limited on-chip resource and power overhead. The experimental results demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed approach under the investigated thermal conditions and indicate its potential engineering value for FPGA temperature monitoring in nuclear safety-class DCSs. Further engineering validation and qualification on target platforms will be required to satisfy the applicable regulatory and certification requirements.
title_ko: 원자력 발전소의 원자력 안전 등급 DCS를 위한 고리 발진기 기반 FPGA 온라인 국소 온도 모니터링

title: Techno-economic optimization of a heat-pipe microreactor, part II: Multi-objective optimization analysis
abstract: Heat-pipe microreactors (HPMRs) are compact and transportable nuclear power systems exhibiting inherent safety, well-suited for deployment in remote regions where access is limited and reliance on costly fossil fuels is prevalent. In prior work, we developed a design optimization framework that incorporates techno-economic considerations through surrogate modeling and reinforcement learning (RL)-based optimization, focusing solely on minimizing the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) by using a bottom-up cost estimation approach. In this study, we extend that framework to a multi-objective optimization that uses the Pareto Envelope Augmented with Reinforcement Learning (PEARL) algorithm. The objectives include minimizing both the rod-integrated peaking factor ( F Δ h ) and LCOE—subject to safety and operational constraints. We evaluate three cost scenarios: (1) a high-cost axial and drum reflectors, (2) a low-cost axial reflector, and (3) low-cost axial and drum reflectors. Our findings indicate that reducing the solid moderator radius, pin pitch, and drum coating angle—all while increasing the fuel height—effectively lowers F Δ h . Across all three scenarios, four key strategies consistently emerged for optimizing LCOE: (1) minimizing the axial reflector contribution when costly, (2) reducing control drum reliance, (3) substituting expensive tri-structural isotropic (TRISO) fuel with axial reflector material priced at the level of graphite, and (4) maximizing fuel burnup. While PEARL demonstrates promise in navigating trade-offs across diverse design scenarios, discrepancies between surrogate model predictions and full-order simulations can lead to infeasibility in some cases, particularly for fuel lifetime and shutdown margin. Therefore, this study should be understood as a surrogate-guided trade-off exploration study rather than an effort to identify exact Pareto-optimal solutions. Further improvements are anticipated through constraint relaxation and surrogate development, constituting an ongoing area of investigation.

title: Monitoring of Dry Cask Storage Systems During Extended Storage
abstract: Nondestructive examination techniques have been studied to support the extended interim storage of spent commercial fuel in dry cask storage systems. Gamma spectroscopy is one option that provides passive interrogation of the radionuclides within the dry storage canister. An elevated signal of 85Kr could indicate a fuel rod failure and evacuation of fission products into the internal void of the canister. A high-purity germanium (HPGe) detector with lead collimation trained on the helium gas gap of the canister could provide sufficient energy resolution to distinguish the 514-keV peak from 85Kr decay.Gamma ray transport is simulated in MCNP using a generic 24 pressurized water reactor dry storage stainless steel canister model with homogenized fuel assemblies in a uniform loading. A F8 tally representing a HPGe with an exaggerated crystal size is used to investigate the distinguishability of the 514-keV signal above the fission product spectrum. The 85Kr signal is quantified with the minimum detectable activity and related to the number of fuel rod failures necessary to detect a change in the internal condition. Simulation results support the feasibility of using the 85Kr signal to identify fuel rod failure for periods of initial license and renewal up to 60 years. Sensitivity analysis is conducted to investigate detectability as a function of the cooling time, burnup, detector location, and shielding thickness.

title: Frequency-Compatible Intensity Measures for Seismic Qualification of Nuclear Power Plant Cabinets Based on a High-Fidelity Numerical Model
abstract: This study develops a high-fidelity nonlinear shell-based finite element model of a full-scale Class 1E electrical cabinet for nuclear power plants (NPPs) and evaluates frequency-compatible intensity measures (IMs) for acceleration-sensitive functional failure. The model explicitly represents realistic cabinet geometry, internal mounting structures, bolted base connections, and mechanically representative contact interfaces and is validated against shaking table test results through modal and transient response comparisons. Five candidate IMs, i.e., peak ground acceleration (PGA), Sā(4–16), Sā(10–20), Sā(20–30), and Sā(10–30), are assessed in terms of sufficiency and fragility-based efficiency. PGA exhibits the strongest residual dependence on frequency content and secondary ground motion parameters, indicating its limited suitability for stiff cabinet response. The conventional spectrum-based IM, Sā(4–16), improves the prediction relative to PGA but does not fully represent the cabinet-relevant high-frequency range. In contrast, the newly examined frequency-compatible IMs reduce both residual dependence and fragility dispersion. Among them, Sā(10–30) provides the weakest dependence on predominant frequency, reducing the fitted slope from −0.067 for PGA to −0.019, and produces the lowest fragility dispersion for the validated cabinet, decreasing the logarithmic standard deviation from approximately 0.50 to 0.21. Sā(10–30) also remains the most efficient of the five candidate IMs for two modified cabinet models with different dynamic characteristics. These findings identify Sā(10–30) as a practical and robust IM for fragility assessment of stiff, acceleration-sensitive NPP electrical cabinets.

title: Dynamic Optimization of Nuclear Expansion in Ontario’s Electricity System with Endogenous Learning Effects
abstract: This paper evaluates the magnitude of future nuclear expansion in the economically optimized 2049 Ontario power mix. A dynamic cost-minimization power mix model is used in conjunction with mixed integer linear programming (MILP) elements to generate several optimized scenarios for power mix expansion over a 25-year period. The linear model uses hourly timesteps to optimize supply management with high time-resolution and multistage decision-making to ensure that endogenous short-term decisions account for future carbon reduction goals and achieve overall cost-minimization. MILP integration provides in-depth analysis of potential future cost reductions that arise from experiential learning in production and deployment processes for new technologies. Multiple scenarios were generated to study optimal system expansion and final power mix composition in 2049 under differing assumptions for learning rates and large nuclear reactor (LN) construction time. The assumed learning rates closely follow technology-specific projections for expected learning effects and, where available, historically demonstrated learning rates. Simulation results show that large reactor focused nuclear expansion is generally encouraged across all candidate scenarios, including the baseline case (no learning assumed). When learning is applied in scenarios, results showed a shifting of system priorities away from current expectations of short-term natural gas (NG) expansion, instead encouraging the construction of additional nuclear technologies and storage systems. Simulated hourly operations, considering seasonal demand changes, showed these alternatives to be capable of providing similar system flexibility to existing gas. When assuming extended construction periods for LN compared to SMRs (10 years versus 5 years) and applying moderate learning rates, scenarios suggest that SMR deployment could be an economically competitive pathway for supply expansion. Under such conditions, early deployment of SMRs is favored to address immediate supply growth needs over other technologies (e.g., NG) and lessens large reactor expansion in the scenario. Through multistage decision-making, results conclude that sufficient learning and short, consistent deployment schedules render SMRs as a cost-effective long-term investment due to impending carbon restrictions, providing incremental supply growth during prolonged construction of larger nuclear projects. Finally, significant grid-scale battery energy storage system (BESS) expansion was observed in high-learning scenarios to provide ramping for system flexibility. BESS inclusion greatly reduced system dependence on continued NG usage for response capabilities but did not significantly impact base-load decision making. All costs in this analysis refer to 2024 CAD unless otherwise specified.
title_ko: 내인성 학습 효과를 이용한 온타리오 전력 시스템의 원자력 확장의 동적 최적화

title: Assessment of the Uncertainty Associated with the Use of Superposition in CANDU Safety Analysis
abstract: There are significant benefits related to Canada deuterium uranium (CANDU) reactors’ capability to fuel the reactor during normal operations including up to 30 months’ operation without an outage, ability to utilize natural uranium-based fuels, and application for use in flux shaping and reactivity management. However, such flexibility also involves rigorous attention to the time-dependent nature of the core, since fueling may introduce local variations in the power distribution that must be demonstrated to fit within the allowable operating limits, and the initial fueling state may affect the behavior of some accident transients. For CANDU safety analysis, this time dependence is sometimes addressed using the “superposition” principle, in which the relative impact of some perturbation to the reactor core is assumed to be the same across different initial core states, greatly simplifying the analysis process but introducing a new source of uncertainty resulting from this assumption. A two-stage study has been completed to examine the sensitivity of key figures of merit in safety simulations to both nuclear data and initial core burnup distribution. First, core follow studies were performed with the PARCS code and reference nuclear data using an emulator that mimicked the decisions of a fueling engineer. Then, using the emulator, studies were performed with 60 nuclear datasets (the aforementioned reference nuclear dataset and 59 randomly selected nuclear datasets from the uncertainty files provide with the SCALE code package). For each of the 60 cases, emulated fueling was performed for 1095 operating days and the important figures of merit were extracted for each day and for each case. The time-dependent figures of merit (liquid zone controller level, maximum channel power, maximum bundle power) were compared across all of the cases and show that the effect of the nuclear data on the distributions of the key parameters was small, mainly resulting from the fueling decisions, which alters the fueling pattern to accommodate any changes in nuclear cross sections. Finally, for each day within each nuclear dataset, a representative failure of a liquid zone controller was introduced and the observed changes in the channel powers and non-failed liquid zone controller responses were observed. These results are then used to assess the uncertainty in the ”superposition” principle utilized in some safety analyses of reactivity device-driven transients to simplify analyses of CANDU reactors. The results of this work quantify the potential uncertainty introduced to safety analysis as a result of the use of superposition on the channel overpower (i.e., the relative increase in each channel power resulting from the liquid zone controller drain) and maximum channel overpower (i.e., the largest relative increase in channel power anywhere in the core resulting from the zone controller drain).

title: Spatial-frequency attention-based neutron radiographic image restoration and quality assessment method
abstract: Neutron radiographic images are often degraded by insufficient beam intensity, exposure time, scattering, detector noise, and collimator size limitations, resulting in low contrast, complex noise, spatial blur, and white spots. Current studies in neutron radiography often treat image restoration and quality assessment as isolated tasks. To achieve a unified framework, we developed a two-step improvement scheme by utilizing the same spatial–frequency attention module and consistent datasets on both the restoration and assessment networks. For the proprietary dataset construction, an updated simulation method for multiple degradations is employed to mitigate the discrepancy between simulated and real-world images. For the network design, centered on the same spatial-frequency attention module, our approach integrates the U-Net-based restoration network with a no-reference image quality assessment network specifically designed for seed screening tasks. Experimental results show that the proposed restoration-assessment scheme significantly enhances the visual quality of authentic neutron radiographic images, thereby providing a potential image-preprocessing method for the subsequent industrial defect detection task.

title: Mapping trapped water in spent nuclear fuel assembly and its internal structures immediately after drainage
abstract: This study quantitatively evaluates the initial residual water remaining after drainage in a pressurized water reactor (PLUS7) fuel assembly, a critical boundary condition determining the efficiency and success of the vacuum drying process in spent nuclear fuel dry storage. To investigate the hydrodynamic trapping mechanisms, multi-mode drainage tests—including gravity drainage, 2 bar compressed air purge, 2 bar helium gas purge, and a hybrid helium purge with a water pump—were conducted on systematically modularized assembly components (top and bottom nozzles, spacer grids, and active fuel rod unit sections). Results demonstrated that simple gravity drainage would leave a massive 8,460.42 ± 20.30 g of water across a full-scale assembly, necessitating active pressurized drainage. The application of a compressed air purge reduced the total residual water to 3,957.00 ± 20.30 g, whereas helium gas purging further decreased it to 3,550.28 ± 20.30 g due to its superior diffusivity and micro-flow-channel penetrability. Notably, the hybrid method combining a downstream water pump and helium gas recorded the lowest total residual water of 3,495.08 ± 20.30 g. Although the pump's hydraulic resistance slightly degraded drainage efficiency in small single components, it significantly extended the flow residence time in the vast active fuel rod sections—which account for over 96% of the trapped water—thereby maximizing the duration of the helium gas's aerodynamic shear force to effectively remove the viscous liquid film. The established quantitative database provides a data-driven operational strategy to minimize residual water, supporting safety evaluations and process reliability for long-term dry storage licensing.

title: Gamma-Ray Shielding, Structural Characterization and Radiation Hazard Assessment of Natural, Compacted, and Calcined Gypsum
abstract: The effects of mechanical compaction and thermal treatment on the gamma-ray shielding performance of natural gypsum collected from South Sinai, Egypt were investigated. Radiological hazard indices were evaluated to assess the radiological safety of the investigated gypsum. Structural and chemical characterization was carried out using X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy (XRF), X-ray diffraction (XRD) and Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) analyses. Gamma-ray attenuation parameters, including the mass attenuation coefficient (MAC), linear attenuation coefficient (LAC), half-value layer (HVL), and mean free path (MFP), were determined experimentally over the energy range 59.53–1408.01 keV and compared with theoretical values obtained from XCOM and Phy-X/PSD. The results showed that mechanical compaction improved the shielding performance by increasing the bulk density, whereas calcination altered the attenuation behavior depending on the treatment temperature. Among all investigated samples, the gypsum compacted at 150 bar exhibited the highest shielding performance. At 662 keV, the LAC increased from 0.132 cm -1 at 50 bar to 0.1826 cm -1 at 150 bar, corresponding to an improvement of approximately 38%. These findings indicate that Egyptian gypsum is a cost-effective material with potential for gamma-ray shielding applications, particularly after mechanical compaction.

title: Measurements, Risk Assessment, and Source Apportionment of Radioactivity Levels in Soil of Okaba and Okobo Coalfields and Environs, Ankpa, Kogi State, Nigeria
abstract: Coal mining can elevate natural radioactivity in surrounding environments, posing radiological risks. This study assessed the activity concentrations of 238U, 232Th, and 40K in 40 composite soil samples collected from active and abandoned mines, waste dumps, farmlands, and residential areas in the Okaba and Okobo coalfields, Kogi State, Nigeria, using high-purity germanium gamma spectrometry. Radiological hazards were evaluated (radium equivalent activity, absorbed dose rates, annual effective doses, hazard indices, annual gonadal equivalent dose, excess lifetime cancer risk), and source apportionment was performed using radionuclide ratios, Pearson correlation, and principal component analysis (PCA).Mean activities (238U: 77.1 Bq·kg−1; 232Th: 81.9 Bq·kg−1; and 40K: 1193 Bq·kg−1) were significantly higher than global averages (p < .001). Ten locations (25%) exceeded the 370 Bq·kg−1 radium equivalent safety limit. The mean absorbed dose rate (570 nGy·h−1) was approximately 10× the global average, and the excess lifetime cancer risk (6.36 × 10−3) exceeded the global reference value (0.29 × 10−3, United Nations Scientific Committee on The Effects of Atomic Radiation report from 2000) by a factor of 20.Source apportionment using PCA with Kaiser criterion (eigenvalues > 1) revealed two dominant sources: geological (66.4% of variance, 232Th and 40K) and anthropogenic mining (31.1%, 238U). The elevated radiological parameters indicate potential long-term health risks, with uranium enrichment linked to artisanal mining activities. Urgent regulatory enforcement is required, aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals 3 (health), 12 (responsible consumption), and 15 (life on land).

title: Development of a Technical, Economic, Risk, and Adoption Assessment Framework for the Evaluation of Modernization Opportunities
abstract: The efficient and cost-effective operation of nuclear power plants is essential for ensuring their long-term economic sustainability and competitiveness. Although the nuclear industry has achieved record high reliability and capacity factors, multiple cost savings and modernization opportunities exist as technology continues to progress. Identifying and objectively screening these opportunities is a periodic and essential plant activity for reducing overall costs and maintaining a modern fleet with up-to-date technology.However, evaluating these opportunities can be challenging for nuclear plant experts and engineers due to the complexity of the plant processes and the constant evolution of new technologies. These challenges often result in the use of costly consultants or potentially the miscalculation of risks or benefits of new technology.To address these challenges, this paper presents the technical, economic, and risk assessment (TERA) framework for screening and evaluating modernization opportunities. This novel framework combines several methodologies, such as process mapping and probabilistic modeling, to help nuclear plants perform quantitative assessments that can aid plant personnel in making risk-informed decisions for technology investments. This novel combination of methodologies creates a systematic evaluation that can reduce investment risk and ensure confidence in the integration of new technologies into existing processes. This paper introduces the TERA framework and presents a case study with initial quantitative results.

title: Transient coupling analysis for helical cruciform fuel core based on 3D method of characteristics and refined subchannel method
abstract: Helical cruciform fuel (HCF) offers enhanced heat transfer, stronger coolant mixing, and improved safety potential for advanced water-cooled reactors, but its complex geometry makes high-fidelity neutronics/thermal-hydraulic (N/TH) coupling analysis challenging. In this study, a coupled framework for HCF cores is developed by integrating the 3D Method of Characteristics code OpenMOC with the refined subchannel code RESTAR-HF. Quarter-core assembly-feedback calculations are first compared with OpenMC/RESTAR-HF results. On this basis, full-core pin-by-pin feedback coupling is performed, and the method is further extended to transient analysis of a rod ejection accident starting from hot full power. For this HFP case, results show that the peak core power reaches 108.451% at 0.04 s, while fuel centerline temperature, clad surface temperature, and minimum departure from nucleate boiling ratio satisfy the predefined criteria for the analyzed transient.
